blocks.content: Module Six closed with a warning: one LoadBalancer Service per application component is expensive and, past a handful of components, unmanageable. This topic opens the object Kubernetes built specifically to fix that, without giving up a single one of LoadBalancer's benefits.
Ingress, Given Its Own Full Depth
blocks.text: Ingress, Given Its Own Full Depth

blocks.content: Ingress is a Kubernetes object that defines HTTP and HTTPS aware routing rules, letting a single external entry point direct traffic to many different backend Services based on the request's URL path or hostname.

Unlike a Service, which operates at the level of raw TCP or UDP connections with no understanding of HTTP request content, an Ingress object reads the actual HTTP request, its host header and its path, and routes accordingly.

This HTTP awareness is the single defining difference from everything covered in the previous module. A Service can tell you which Pod to send a connection to. An Ingress can tell you which Service to send a connection to based on what the request is actually asking for.

An Ingress object, by itself, is purely declarative, a list of routing rules written in YAML. The next topic covers exactly what makes those rules actually take effect, but this topic focuses entirely on what the rules themselves express.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643036264-383916331.png
blocks.alt: Ingress given its own full depth

blocks.content: One Load Balancer, Many Applications

The core value proposition of Ingress is consolidation: instead of provisioning a separate cloud load balancer for every application component, as a naive LoadBalancer Service approach would require, a single load balancer sits in front of an Ingress controller.

That one load balancer receives all external traffic for every application behind it, and the Ingress rules, evaluated by the controller, determine which specific Service each individual request should actually be forwarded to.

This is a direct, structural solution to the exact cost problem raised as a common mistake in the LoadBalancer topic: a cluster with twenty microservices no longer needs twenty separate, separately billed cloud load balancers.

Instead, that same cluster needs exactly one load balancer in front of the Ingress controller, plus as many Ingress objects, or as many rules within a single Ingress object, as there are distinct routing needs among those twenty microservices.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643038371-686789955.png
blocks.alt: One load balancer fronting many applications

blocks.content: A Real Multi Application Example

Consider a company running three separate applications on one cluster: a marketing website, a customer facing API, and an internal admin dashboard, each with its own Deployment and its own ClusterIP Service.

A single Ingress object defines three rules: requests to www.example.com go to the marketing website's Service, requests to api.example.com go to the API's Service, and requests to admin.example.com go to the dashboard's Service.

All three domains resolve in public DNS to the exact same external IP address, the one address belonging to the single load balancer sitting in front of the Ingress controller, with the Ingress rules doing the actual internal sorting.

Adding a fourth application later requires only adding one more rule to the Ingress object, and possibly one more DNS record, without provisioning any new cloud infrastructure or paying for any additional load balancer.

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: company-ingress
spec:
  rules:
    - host: www.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: marketing-site
                port:
                  number: 80
    - host: api.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: api-service
                port:
                  number: 80

blocks.content: Recap: The Cost Problem Ingress Solves
blocks.text: Recap: The Cost Problem Ingress Solves

blocks.content: The LoadBalancer topic in the previous module explicitly warned against creating one LoadBalancer Service per application component, precisely because each one is a separately billed, separately managed cloud resource.

That warning ended with a promise: for cases where multiple externally facing paths genuinely are needed behind a single address, an Ingress controller is almost always the more cost effective and more manageable solution.

This topic is that promise delivered in full. Every specific cost and management concern raised there is directly and structurally addressed by consolidating routing decisions into Ingress rules behind one shared entry point.

Reading this topic as the direct continuation of that earlier warning, rather than as an unrelated new object, is the correct way to understand exactly why Ingress exists and why it sits naturally as the very next module after Services.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643041731-668882399.png
blocks.alt: Recap of the one load balancer per Service mistake

blocks.content: HTTP Awareness: The Capability a Service Cannot Offer
blocks.text: HTTP Awareness: The Capability a Service Cannot Offer

blocks.content: A Service, at its core, is a Layer 4 mechanism, operating purely on IP addresses and ports, with genuinely no visibility into the content of the traffic flowing through it, whether that traffic happens to be HTTP, a database protocol, or anything else.

An Ingress operates at Layer 7, meaning it actually parses the HTTP request, reading the Host header to determine hostname based routing and reading the URL path to determine path based routing, both covered in their own full depth later in this module.

This distinction is precisely why Ingress could never simply be built as another Service type. Routing based on HTTP request content is a fundamentally different kind of capability from anything a Layer 4 Service, no matter its type, was ever designed to express.

Recognizing this Layer 4 versus Layer 7 distinction clearly is the single most useful mental model for understanding not just what Ingress does, but why it had to be introduced as an entirely separate kind of Kubernetes object.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643043523-470441689.png
blocks.alt: HTTP aware routing by path and host together

blocks.content: Ingress Is Not Automatically Available

Unlike core objects such as Pods, Deployments, and Services, which are always available on any conformant Kubernetes cluster, the Ingress object type itself is part of the core API, but acting on it requires additional software to be installed separately.

This distinction between an API object existing and that object having any real effect is genuinely important, and it is the direct setup for the very next topic, which covers exactly what software is required to make Ingress rules actually work.

A newly created cluster, particularly a fresh local development cluster, very often has no Ingress controller installed by default, meaning any Ingress object created on it will simply sit inert, defining rules that nothing is currently enforcing.

This gap catches many engineers by surprise the first time they encounter Ingress, expecting it to behave like a Service that works immediately upon creation, rather than requiring one additional, deliberate installation step first.
A Common Mistake: No Controller Installed
blocks.text: A Common Mistake: No Controller Installed

blocks.content: A frequent early mistake is writing a perfectly correct Ingress manifest, applying it with kubectl, and then being confused when external traffic still cannot reach the application, because no Ingress controller was ever installed on the cluster.

The Ingress object itself was created successfully, and kubectl get ingress shows it exists, but with no controller watching for it, the routing rules it defines are never actually translated into real, working network configuration.

This mistake is easy to diagnose once recognized: an Ingress object with no external address ever populated in its status, persisting well past the couple of minutes cloud provisioning would normally take, is a strong signal no controller is watching it.

The fix, covered fully in the next topic, is installing an Ingress controller appropriate for the cluster's environment, at which point existing Ingress objects begin working correctly without needing to be recreated.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643045370-54586514.png
blocks.alt: The mistake of creating Ingress with no controller installed

blocks.content: Ingress Compared to a Reverse Proxy
blocks.text: Ingress Compared to a Reverse Proxy

blocks.content: Engineers with prior experience running a reverse proxy such as NGINX or HAProxy in front of a traditional application will find Ingress conceptually familiar: a single entry point routing requests to different backends based on host and path.

The genuine difference is that Ingress expresses this routing declaratively, as Kubernetes native YAML, continuously reconciled against the cluster's actual state, rather than as a manually maintained configuration file requiring a manual reload on every change.

This declarative nature means Ingress rules can be version controlled, code reviewed, and deployed through the exact same GitOps or CI CD pipelines already used for every other Kubernetes object covered throughout this course.

For engineers making this transition, thinking of Ingress as a Kubernetes native reverse proxy configuration is a genuinely useful starting mental model, even though the underlying implementation details differ meaningfully from a traditional standalone reverse proxy.
The Structure of an Ingress Manifest
blocks.text: The Structure of an Ingress Manifest

blocks.content: An Ingress manifest's spec centers on a rules array, where each rule optionally specifies a host and always specifies one or more HTTP paths, each path mapped to a specific backend Service and port.

A rule with no host specified acts as a catch all for any hostname not matched by a more specific rule, a behavior worth understanding clearly since it interacts directly with the default backend concept covered later in this module.

Each path entry also specifies a pathType, most commonly Prefix, indicating that the rule matches any URL beginning with the given path, which is the path based routing mechanism given its own full dedicated depth two topics from now.

This structure, hosts containing paths containing backends, is the complete shape of nearly every real world Ingress manifest, and internalizing it now makes every subsequent topic in this module significantly easier to follow.

{"headers":["Field","Purpose"],"rows":[["rules","List of routing rules evaluated in order"],["host","Optional hostname to match against the request"],["paths","URL path prefixes within a given host"],["backend","The Service and port a matching request is sent to"]]}
Where Ingress Fits in the Module Sequence
blocks.text: Where Ingress Fits in the Module Sequence

blocks.content: This module is deliberately sequenced to mirror how a real engineer actually needs this knowledge: first understand what Ingress is and why it exists, then understand the controller that makes it work, then understand the two core routing mechanisms.

Path based routing and host based routing, covered as the next two full topics after the controller topic, are the two primary tools every Ingress rule is built from, and mastering both is what makes writing a correct Ingress manifest genuinely straightforward.

TLS, Default Backend, and the final comparison against LoadBalancer close out the module, rounding out the practical, production ready picture of everything a real Ingress deployment actually needs beyond the routing rules themselves.

Following this sequence closely, rather than skipping ahead, builds the same kind of layered, connected understanding that the Services module built for ClusterIP, NodePort, and LoadBalancer, each topic depending directly on the one before it.
Ingress and the Broader Object Model
blocks.text: Ingress and the Broader Object Model

blocks.content: Ingress fits the same declarative, controller reconciled pattern already familiar from every object covered so far in this course: a manifest describes desired routing intent, and a separate controller continuously works to make that intent real.

This consistency is deliberate on Kubernetes's part. Learning any single object deeply, whether a Deployment, a Service, or now an Ingress, transfers directly into understanding the shape of every other object, since they all share this same underlying reconciliation model.

Recognizing Ingress as another instance of this familiar pattern, rather than a fundamentally different kind of object requiring an entirely new mental model, is what makes the rest of this module considerably easier to absorb.

Every remaining topic in this module builds on this same foundation: a manifest declares intent, a controller, covered next, makes it real, and the specific rules within that manifest determine exactly what real behavior results.
Ingress in a Typical Application Lifecycle
blocks.text: Ingress in a Typical Application Lifecycle

blocks.content: A typical new application's path to production, on a cluster already running an Ingress controller, looks like this: a Deployment and a ClusterIP Service are created first, then an Ingress rule is added pointing a chosen host or path at that Service.

This ordering matters. An Ingress rule referencing a Service that does not yet exist is not an error, but it also has no effect until that Service is actually created, mirroring the same selector matching behavior already covered for Endpoints in the previous module.

Once all three pieces exist together, Deployment, Service, and Ingress rule, the application becomes reachable through the shared entry point, with no separate load balancer provisioning step required specifically for that one application.

This complete lifecycle, from Deployment through Service through Ingress rule, is worth internalizing as a single, repeatable pattern applied to every new HTTP based application deployed to the cluster from this point forward.
Why This Module Follows Directly After Services
blocks.text: Why This Module Follows Directly After Services

blocks.content: This module's placement immediately after the Services module is deliberate, not incidental. Every Ingress rule ultimately points at a backend Service, meaning genuine fluency with Services is a direct prerequisite for genuine fluency with Ingress.

The selector matching, the Endpoints tracking, and the DNS based discovery covered throughout the Services module all continue operating exactly as already learned, entirely underneath and independently of whatever Ingress rules happen to sit in front of them.

Ingress adds a new layer on top of that existing foundation. It does not replace or change any of it, which is precisely why this module has repeatedly referenced concepts from the Services module rather than introducing an entirely separate, disconnected set of ideas.

Keeping this layered relationship clear, Ingress on top of Services on top of Pods, is the single most useful way to reason about how a real HTTP request actually travels from the public internet down to the specific container that ultimately handles it.
A Quick Mental Checklist for Choosing Ingress
blocks.text: A Quick Mental Checklist for Choosing Ingress

blocks.content: Before defaulting to a LoadBalancer Service for a new application, a short mental checklist helps confirm whether Ingress is actually the better fit: is the traffic HTTP or HTTPS, are there multiple applications that could share one entry point, and is cost consolidation valuable.

If the answer to all three is yes, Ingress is almost certainly the right tool. If the traffic is not HTTP, for example a raw TCP database connection or a UDP based protocol, Ingress cannot help, and LoadBalancer or NodePort remains the correct choice instead.

This checklist is deliberately short, mirroring the similar checklist introduced in the very first topic of the previous module, and it is worth running through consciously for every new application before defaulting to whichever mechanism was used most recently.

The final topic of this module returns to this exact checklist in far more detail, offering a complete, structured comparison between Ingress and LoadBalancer once every piece of Ingress has been covered in full.

blocks.content: The Single Most Valuable Takeaway

Ingress exists to solve a real, concrete problem directly inherited from the end of the previous module: too many load balancers, too much cost, and too little HTTP awareness in the routing layer of a growing application.
It does this by introducing a genuinely new kind of routing intelligence, HTTP aware, host and path sensitive, that no Service type, no matter how it is configured, was ever designed to provide.

The next topic gives the Ingress controller, the piece of software that actually makes every Ingress rule real, the full dedicated treatment already promised twice in this topic, closing the one remaining gap in understanding how any of this actually works end to end.

Keep the one load balancer, many applications image firmly in mind. Every remaining topic in this module is really just a deeper explanation of exactly how that one load balancer knows where to send each individual request.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643047041-488101010.png

blocks.title: What Is Ingress, In Full
points: Ingress defines HTTP and HTTPS aware routing rules, directing traffic to different Services based on request host and path, something no Service type alone can express.

Its core value is consolidation: one load balancer and one Ingress controller can front many applications, directly solving the one load balancer per Service cost problem raised in the previous module.
An Ingress object alone has no effect without an Ingress controller installed and watching for it, a genuinely common early point of confusion.
Ingress manifests are structured as hosts containing paths containing backend Service references, a shape worth internalizing before the next several topics.
The Ingress Controller, covered next, is the piece of software that actually reads and enforces every Ingress rule covered conceptually in this topic.
